title: Cookie Clicker Clone
tagline: An incremental game used as a case study: modular Clean Architecture, strict MVC and TDD in Unity.
overview: A recreation of the core mechanics of [Cookie Clicker](https://cookieclicker.com/). It is a practice project whose goal is **architecture and code quality**, not visual polish.

Incremental games are a great domain-modeling exercise: production, exponential progression and dynamic prices are deterministic and don't depend on the engine, so domain and presentation separate cleanly.

highlights.title: Core loop
highlights.text: Click the cookie, buy buildings and watch the cookies-per-second grow every frame.

highlights.title: Two shops
highlights.text: Buildings with dynamic prices that reveal new ones as you progress, and upgrades that boost production globally or per building type.

highlights.title: Unlock conditions
highlights.text: Every upgrade defines when it becomes available and only shows up when those conditions are met.

decisions.title: Modular Clean Architecture
decisions.text: Instead of one monolithic domain, the game is split by feature: **Cookies**, **Store** and **Modifiers**. Each module has a pure C# **Domain** and an **Infrastructure** layer with the Unity-specific code.

decisions.title: Modules isolated with assemblies
decisions.text: Unity assembly definitions prevent cyclic dependencies and keep the domain independent from the engine at compile time.

decisions.title: Passive views, thin controllers
decisions.text: MVC for the shops and the cookie view. Controllers listen to the UI, call the domain and hand results to the view through DTOs. Views implement interfaces such as `IBuildingStoreView`, following dependency inversion.

decisions.title: TDD where it matters
decisions.text: The domain is covered by tests for costs, production per second, upgrade effects and unlock conditions, written test first.

learnings: Strict MVC doesn't map naturally onto Unity's component model. For values that change every frame (cookies, production, prices), an **observer pattern** would have been cleaner than DTOs. I'd do that differently next time.
Patterns need to justify themselves: the balance between architectural discipline and over-engineering.
If I extended it, the next step would be an editor tool to manage buildings and upgrades, which are currently configured by hand across several ScriptableObjects.
